frames.narration: A helper library has four hazards: two booleans in a row, a destructive default, a getter that creates things, and a name that hides an in-place change. 20 callers use it. Some read names only, some the signature, a few the docs.

A caller writes delete('/a'), believing the directory is empty. The name says delete, the default says recursive. 2 files are gone. get_user('zed') makes a user that did not exist, and export(rows, true, false) swaps header and compression without any error.

states.impl: does more than the name says

frames.narration: How many callers bite depends on how much they read. With this mix, 56 calls are mistaken and the damage is 168 points. The destructive default alone is 80 of them.

A hurried team, mostly reading names only, makes 73 mistaken calls and 206 points of damage. A careful team that reads the docs makes 15 and 50. The interface is the same: it is safe only for those who read the most.

The least astonishing version fixes the cause. delete refuses a non-empty directory unless recursive is stated. find_user reads, ensure_user creates. Options are named. sorted_copy returns a copy. The hazards are visible in the call itself.

A call stays short: 2 arguments for the common case, and the rare dangerous act is spelled out. The mistaken calls drop to 0 in the model, and the damage with them. Real callers still err, but they cannot get there by accident.

The over-applied extreme: every option must be spelled out, with confirmations, 14 arguments per call. Callers who read names only paste the settings from the nearest example, so for the dangerous operations 16 calls are still mistaken, with 64 points of damage.
The rule: make the common case short and obvious, give each behaviour a name that says what it does, make the default harmless, and make the dangerous case explicit, but only that one.
